subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Front, Rear, and All-Wheel Drive
description: A quick, practical guide to Front, Rear, and All-Wheel Drive.

hook.text: Which wheels get the engine's power changes how a car handles, grips, and even wears its tires.

buildup.text: Front-wheel drive is cheap and space-efficient. The engine and transmission sit together up front.

discovery.text: Rear-wheel drive gives better weight balance and handling, which is why sports cars prefer it.

twist.text: All-wheel drive sends power to all four wheels but adds weight, complexity, and cost.

climax.text: AWD helps in rain and snow but won't save you from bad tires—grip starts at the rubber.

punchline.text: Drive type shapes how a car behaves, not just where.

quiz.question: Why do sports cars often use rear-wheel drive?

details.summary: Drivetrain layout determines which wheels receive engine power. Front-wheel drive is efficient and compact, rear-wheel drive balances handling, and all-wheel drive maximizes traction in all conditions.
details.whyItMatters: The choice of drivetrain affects handling, fuel economy, cost, and capability in different weather and terrain, making it one of the most important decisions when buying a vehicle.
takeaways: Front-wheel drive puts the engine and transaxle up front
Rear-wheel drive offers better handling balance for performance
All-wheel drive distributes power to all four wheels dynamically

faq.question: Is all-wheel drive always better than front-wheel drive?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. AWD adds weight, cost, and complexity while reducing fuel economy. For most drivers on paved roads, good winter tires on a FWD car provide comparable traction at lower cost.

faq.question: Why do sports cars prefer rear-wheel drive?
faq.answer: Rear-wheel drive separates steering from power delivery, reducing torque steer. Under acceleration, weight transfers to the rear axle, improving traction exactly where power is applied.
